A standard measure of the approximate number sense: judging which group is larger too fast to count, where the difficulty is the ratio between them.
A standard measure of visual short-term memory span: the longest sequence of positions you can reproduce in order.
A standard measure of sustained divided attention: how many moving targets you can keep hold of among identical distractors.
A standard measure of spatial ability: deciding whether two figures are the same solid turned, or mirror images that no rotation can match.
A standard measure of working memory: holding a sequence while an unrelated task occupies the same mental workspace.

A standard measure of cognitive flexibility: the cost of dropping the rule you were just using and applying a different one.
A standard measure of working memory updating: keeping a running window of the last few items current, and judging against it while it keeps moving.
A standard measure of planning: the puzzle needs moves that undo progress before the goal can be reached.

Counting on, sums to 20, and tens and ones.
Find any number on the number line.
One step right is one more. One step left is one less.
Counting on is adding. Watch three hops land on ten.
Start at 12 and count on four hops.
13, 14, 15, 16 - four hops to the right lands on 16.
Skip counting means jumping by the same amount each time instead of one by one. These jumps are all ten.
Each jump adds the same amount. Keep going.
Counting back moves one step left, so 40 becomes 39, not 30.
Make ten, and count back to subtract.
Ten is the easy number, so fill the frame up to ten first.
The frame holds ten and {a:7} are filled, so {b:3} squares are still empty.
Fill the ten first, then add what is left over.
{a:8} needs {b:2} to reach ten, and {b:3} of the {b:5} are left over.
Taking away hops back the same way: down to ten first, then the rest.
Hop back to ten first, then hop what is left.
Same trick, one bigger hop back.
A two-digit number is rods of ten plus loose ones.
How many rods of ten are here?
The question counts the rods, not what they are worth: {a:six} rods, worth {a:60}.
Add the rods: {a:2} tens and {b:1} ten make 3 tens.
{a:4} rods is {a:40}, and {b:2} loose ones make 42.
Compare the rods first. {a:Seven} rods beat {b:four}, so the ones never get a say.
Both have the same rods, so the loose ones decide. Which is larger?
The rods tie at six each, so the loose ones decide it, and {b:8} beats {a:3}.
Each jump adds ten, so the one after 40 is 50.
9 takes 1 of the 6 to make ten, and the other 5 carry on past it.
Hop back four to land on ten, and the last two hops reach 8.
How many loose ones are here?
The loose ones are the single cubes, so three; the five rods are worth 50.
26 has two rods against six, so it is the smaller whatever its loose ones do.
These jumps are all the same size. What comes next?
Each jump adds five, not one, so 25 + 5 = 30.
Equal rows, the facts that fall out of them, and sharing back out.
Rows and columns make the times tables make sense.
Multiplication is equal rows. Count how many rows, count what is in each, and the dots do the rest.
Turn the array on its side and not one dot is lost, so every fact you learn hands you a second one free.
Counting the rows on is skip counting: one row of three, then two rows, then three.
Lay {a:3} rows down twice and the total doubles, because the second block is a copy of the first.
A baking tray holds {a:4} rows of {b:7} cakes.
Break a hard times fact into two easy ones.
Nobody counts seven rows one dot at a time. Take the {a:5} rows everyone knows, then add the {b:2} that are left.
Fives are the easy ones, so peel off {a:5} rows first.
Ten rows is the easiest count of all: the number with a nought written after it.
Ten rows of six would be 60, and this array is one row short of that.
One row of six comes back off the sixty: 60 - 6 = 54.
{a:5} rows of eight, and {b:2} more rows of eight.
{a:5} eights are {a:40} and {b:2} more are {b:16}, so the array holds 56.
Double the {a:2} rows, then double the answer.
Nine doubled is 18, and 18 doubled is 36.
Division undoes multiplication, and sometimes leaves a bit over.
Division takes the total back apart into equal rows. It is the same array, read the other way round.
Every times fact hands you two division facts, because the array can be cut either way.
How many rows of eight does it take?
Eight sevens are 56, so 56 splits into exactly seven rows of eight.
Not every total shares out evenly. Whatever will not fill another row is the remainder.
Deal them out in rows of {b:4}.
{b:1} sweet will not make an eighth row.
A crate holds {b:5} bottles. How many crates can you fill from 38 bottles?
{a:Seven} full rows of {b:five}, and {b:three} bottles with nowhere to go.
Eight rows of seven, and eight sevens are 56.
Five nines is 45, and one more nine makes 54.
Which has the same total as 7 x 4?
Turning the array on its side changes nothing.
Counting on in nines reaches 72 in exactly eight hops.
Counting on in fours reaches 20 in five hops, and 3 is left over.
A tray holds 8 rows of 6 buns. How many buns?
Five sixes is 30 and three more sixes is 18, so the tray holds 48.
What the two numbers mean, matching them up, and adding them.
What each of the two numbers is for.
The bottom number says how many equal pieces the bar was cut into. The top number says how many of them you take.
Two shaded out of five pieces in all, so the five goes underneath.
The more pieces the bar is cut into, the thinner each piece gets. An eighth is a narrower slice than a quarter.
Same bottom number, so the pieces are the same size: {b:five} of them beats {a:three}.
A cake is cut into 8 slices and 3 are eaten. How many eighths are still on the plate?
{b:Three} of the eight pieces are gone, so 5/8 of the cake is left.
Which of these is a whole one?
Take every piece there is and you have the whole bar back.
Different names for exactly the same amount.
Cut every piece in half and you get twice as many, each half the size. The shading never moved.
Whatever you do to the bottom you do to the top, and the amount stays exactly where it was.
Which fraction shades the same amount as this bar?
Doubling both numbers renames 2/3 as 4/6 without moving the shading.
Cancelling runs the trick backwards: divide top and bottom by the same number and the fraction gets a simpler name.
Cut both into twelfths and they are {a:8/12} against {b:9/12}.
How many tenths shade the same as this bar?
Both numbers doubled: five pieces become ten, three become six.
Same-size pieces add; different ones have to be matched first.
Pieces of the same size simply add: {a:3} fifths and {b:1} fifth are four fifths. The pieces never change size, so the bottom number never changes either.
The pieces already match, so add the tops and leave the bottom alone.
Two sevenths and three sevenths are five sevenths. Nothing was cut any thinner.
Taking away works the same way. Five sixths with two sixths gone leaves three of them.
Pieces of different sizes cannot be added as they stand. Rename one bar until both are cut the same way.
A half and a quarter are different sizes, so nothing can be added yet.
Cut the half into quarters: {a:1}/2 is {a:2}/4.
Now both bars are in quarters.
Sixths and thirds. Match the pieces first.
{b:1/3} is {b:2/6}, so the sum is 3/6, which is one half.
The bottom number counts all five pieces, the top counts the two shaded.
Which fraction shades the same as this bar?
4 is half of 8, and half the bar is shaded.
A half is 4/8, and four eighths beat three.
The pieces are the same size, so only the tops add.
Two of the five shaded sixths go, and the pieces stay sixths.
A half is two quarters, and two quarters plus one more is 3/4.
Reading, comparing and adding the places past the point.
Place value carries on past the point.
The square is one whole. A column of it is a tenth, and a single cell is a hundredth.
A fraction and a decimal can be the very same amount, written two ways.
The nought is not decoration. It holds the tenths place empty so the 5 lands in hundredths.
A cent is a hundredth of a euro, and the nought keeps the tenths empty.
How much of the square is shaded?
Four whole columns, and a column is a tenth, so 0.4 and not 0.04.
A longer decimal is not a bigger one.
Compare the tenths first. Only when those tie do the hundredths get a say.
{a:Four} tenths beats {b:three} tenths. Extra digits do not make a number bigger.
Writing a nought on the end changes nothing at all: the same cells are shaded either way.
Money is a decimal you already read without thinking. Half a euro is fifty of its hundred cents.
How many hundredths shade the same as this square?
Three columns of ten cells each, so 0.3 is 30 hundredths.
Smallest first. Which order is right?
{a:0.09} has no tenths at all, so it is the smallest however long it looks.
Tenths onto tenths, hundredths onto hundredths.
Adding decimals is adding same-sized pieces, exactly as fractions do: {a:4} tenths take on {b:35} hundredths.
Write {a:0.6} as {a:0.60} so both numbers reach the hundredths.
Line the points up, then add one column at a time.
Write 0.3 as 0.30, then five hundredths and seven tenths make 0.75.
A subtraction is the same picture read backwards: {a:35} hundredths are already there, and {b:4} tenths bring it back up to 0.75.
A pencil costs 0.45 euro and a rubber 0.30 euro. What do they cost together?
Forty-five cents and thirty cents make seventy-five.
How much more shading would fill the square?
35 cells are shaded, so 65 of the hundred are not.
Five tenths beats four tenths and five hundredths.
0.08 has no tenths at all, so it sits below every number here that has one.
Write 0.4 as 0.40, then tenths onto tenths and hundredths onto hundredths give 0.65.
Which fraction is the same amount as 0.25?
25 hundredths is one quarter of the square.
0.70 take away 0.35 leaves half of it.
Below zero, and what the two signs do to each other.
The line carries on, and so does the order.
Zero is not the end of the line. Right is still more and left is still less, and to the left of zero the numbers wear a minus.
A negative is a shortfall, not a quantity. Minus four is four steps below zero, and there is nothing you can have four of.
Furthest right on the line wins, and zero sits to the right of every negative.
The further left, the smaller. That is why -10 is less than -1, even though 10 is more than 1.
A freezer sits at -18 degrees and a fridge at -2. Which is colder?
-18 is further left, so it is the smaller number and the colder one.
How many degrees warmer is the fridge than the freezer?
From -18 up to -2 is 16 steps, which is why the two minus signs come out positive.
Hopping across zero, and what two minus signs do.
Adding moves right and taking away moves left. Crossing zero changes nothing about that.
Hop up to zero first, then carry on.
{b:7} of the twelve get you to zero, and the other {b:5} carry on past it.
The temperature is -4 and drops six more.
Six steps left of {a:-4} lands on -10.
Taking away a negative moves right, the same way adding does, because losing a debt leaves you better off.
Two minus signs in a row cancel each other out.
Taking away {b:-9} moves nine steps right of {a:-2}, which lands on 7.
Adding a negative is the other half of the same rule: it moves left, so the two signs collapse into one.
Why two negatives make a positive.
Three lots of a debt is a bigger debt, so a negative times a positive stays negative.
Three rows of a debt of six.
Walk a times table down past zero: 3 lots of -4, then 2, then 1, then none. Every step adds the same {b:4}, so once the first number goes negative the answers have to carry on up into the positives.
That is the whole of the rule. Two signs the same give a positive, two different give a negative, and division behaves exactly as multiplication does.
Both signs are the same here.
Thirty shares into sixes five times, and matching signs give a positive.
Divide first, then decide the sign.
Forty-five shares into nines five times, and the two signs differ, so the answer is negative.
Six of the nine carry you to zero, and the other three carry on past it to 3.
Furthest left is smallest, so -9 is below -2 even though 9 is more than 2.
Taking away moves left, and eight steps left of -3 is -11.
Taking away a negative moves right, so this is 7 + 5.
Each step up the ladder adds five, so past zero the answers turn positive.
Thirty-six shares into nines four times, and the signs differ, so it is -4.
Counting parts against parts, sharing them out, and scaling them up.
Parts against parts, not parts against the whole.
A ratio counts parts against parts, not parts against the whole. One part to four parts is one in every five, not one in four.
Cut every part again and the mix is unchanged: more pieces, each one smaller, the same two colours side by side.
The bar is {a:6} against {b:9}, and both divide by three.
A ratio carries no units and no total. {a:Two} to {b:three} describes the mix whether the bucket holds 5 litres or 500.
{a:One} part sand to {b:three} parts gravel. What fraction of the mix is sand?
One part out of the four parts in the bar, which is exactly the trap a ratio sets.
How many parts are there altogether in this bar?
Counting the parts is always the first move, because it is what one part gets measured against.
Count the parts, price one part, hand them out.
To share in a ratio, count the parts first, then work out what a single part is worth.
Share 80 euro in the ratio {a:3} : {b:1}. What is the larger share?
Four parts of 20 euro, and the larger share takes three of them.
There is no reason to stop at two parts. Three to two to one is six parts, and the method does not change.
Share 180 g in the ratio {a:3} : {b:2} : {a:1}. How many grams are in the largest share?
Six parts of 30 g, and the largest share takes three of them.
A {a:2} : {b:3} mix holds 12 litres of the first colour. How much of the second?
Two parts are 12, so one part is 6, and the second colour takes three of them.
Find what one is worth, then multiply.
In direct proportion, double one amount and the other doubles with it.
Work out what a single one is worth first. That one step answers every scaling question there is.
Rice for 4 people is 300 g. How much for 6?
One person needs {a:75} g, so {b:6} of them need 450 g.
8 pens cost 6 euro. What do 12 cost?
Four pens cost 3 euro, and twelve is three fours.
A map is drawn to a scale of 1 : 50000. A road measures 4 cm on it.
Every 1 cm on the map stands for {b:50000} cm on the ground.
Not everything scales that way. Two painters take half the time rather than twice as long, which is inverse proportion.
The first colour takes three parts and the second five, in that order.
In the ratio {a:2} : {b:7}, what fraction of the whole is the first part?
Two parts out of the nine in the bar, not out of the seven.
Share 100 euro in the ratio {a:1} : {b:4}. What is the smaller share?
Five parts of 20 euro, and the smaller share takes one.
Both sides divide by five, and 3 : 5 will not go any further.
A recipe for 6 people uses 240 g of flour. How much for 9?
240 g shared by 6 is 40 g each, so 9 people take 360 g.
A model is built to a scale of 1 : 200. How tall is the model of a 30 m tower, in cm?
30 m is 3000 cm, and 3000 shared into 200 is 15 cm.
Parts of a hundred: taking them, adding them on, and working them out.
A percentage is a hundred-square with some of it shaded.
Per cent means out of a hundred, so a percentage is a hundred-square with some of its squares shaded.
A percentage, a decimal and a fraction are three names for one amount of shading.
To take a percentage of an amount, share the amount over the hundred squares and count the shaded ones.
50% is one half of anything, and half of 64 is 32.
Ten per cent first, then half of it again.
{a:10}% is {b:20} and {a:5}% is half of that, so {a:15}% comes to 30.
0.4 is 40 squares out of the hundred, and nothing else on the list reaches that.
Adding it on, taking it off
Rises, discounts, and why they do not cancel.
An increase adds the percentage on top; a decrease takes it off.
A 40 euro jacket is 25% off. What do you pay?
A quarter of {b:40} is {a:10}, and that {a:10} is what comes off.
One multiplication does it in a single step, because 20% off is the same as keeping 80%.
A 60 euro fare rises by 15%. What is the new fare, in euro?
15% of {a:60} is 9, and that goes on top.
Up 10%, then down 10%. Where do you end up?
The rise was 10% of 100, but the fall is 10% of {b:110}, which is 11. More comes off than went on.
That is the whole reason they never cancel: the second percentage is taken of a different number from the first.
Measure the change against what you started from.
To find what percentage one number is of another, divide the one by the other and multiply by a hundred.
Measure it against the original, not the new price.
Always measure against what you started from. Against the new price you would get a different answer to a different question.
A price falls from 80 to 60. What is the percentage decrease?
The change is 20, and 20 against the original 80 is 0.25.
A test is marked 18 out of 24. What percentage is that?
18 out of 24 is three quarters of the paper.
A shop's takings go from 200 to 250. By what percentage did they rise?
10% of 150 is 15 and 2% is 3, so 12% is 18.
75% is three quarters, and three quarters of 40 is 30.
Which of these is the same amount as 45%?
Per cent means out of a hundred, so 45% is 45 hundredths: 0.45.
A 90 euro coat is 30% off. What do you pay?
30% of 90 is 27, and that is what comes off.
A price rises from 40 to 50. What is the percentage increase?
100 euro goes up 20%, then down 20%. What is left?
The rise is 20% of 100, but the fall is 20% of 120, which is 24.
Huge and tiny numbers written as one digit and a power of ten.
One digit and a power of ten
Counting jumps instead of counting noughts.
Every jump along this line multiplies by ten. Counting the jumps is quicker than counting noughts, and that count is the power.
The front number always sits between 1 and 10. 52 is three jumps below 52 000, so 5.2 is four, and four is the power.
Two of these are the right digits in the wrong shape.
72 and 0.72 are outside the 1 to 10 window. From 7.2 the point moves five places.
The power counts jumps, so it decides the size long before the front number gets a say. Anything times a bigger power of ten wins.
Walk the point three jumps to the right.
All four have the right digits. Only one is in standard form and worth 12 000.
12 and 0.12 are outside the window, and 1.2 * 10^3 is only 1 200.
The same line walked backwards, with negative powers.
Small numbers are the same line walked backwards. Each step divides by ten, and the power counts those steps as negatives: 6, 0.6, 0.06, 0.006.
The minus in the power says which way to walk, not that the number is negative. A number in standard form is negative only when the front number is.
Count the jumps from 8.2 down to this number.
Four steps left of 8.2, and 82 is outside the 1 to 10 window.
Walk the point four jumps to the left.
A negative front number and a negative power mean two different things, and either can happen without the other.
The most negative power walks furthest left, so it is the smallest.
Only one of these has a power of -4, and 0.0009 is below every other number here.
The two halves travel separately. The front numbers multiply with each other, and the powers of ten add.
The powers of ten add: 10^4 x 10^3 = 10^7.
Put the two halves back together.
Dividing runs it backwards: the front numbers divide and the powers subtract.
The front number can come out of the multiplication too big for the window, and then it has to be walked back in.
The front numbers give 20, which is outside the window.
20 * 10^5 has the right value in the wrong shape: walk the point one place left and the power goes up one.
How many times bigger is 8 * 10^7 than 8 * 10^4?
The front numbers match, so only the three extra jumps count.
Which one is 45 000 in standard form?
